HR PUFNSTUF was a puppet series that ran for one season (17 episodes) in 1969.  It was later syndicated, and those 17 episodes appeared for several more years.

As I was already 13 when it first ran, I never watched the show.  But it was still a gimme because the ridiculous name was quite eye-catching when looking at the listings in the TV Guide (remember those?).

So for me, it was a gimme, but I can imagine it might be a no-know for younger solvers.  Luckily, all the crosses were super common.

The same older vibe is shared by JR EWING, whose attempted assassination took place about a decade later, though even those too young to have been watching (or even not born yet) might have heard of the fictional oil baron, since it was a much bigger TV event, dragged out as a (word from the Midi) over the summer of 1980.

(Apparently, in 2013, in a reboot of the original series, JR was not only shot but killed, but no one remembers that.)

All this by way of saying that I can see how younger solvers might be a bit slowed down in these two places, but for older solvers, there might be some record times today.

I recall that one of our sons ran for president of his junior class (a large, raucous, city highschool) against a pseudonymous no-show who signed up to run as H.R. Pufnstuf -- and of course my son lost by a few votes (he was delighted and thought it a big lark), and the junior class never did find out who their class president was. Turns out H.R. is a dragon, although there has been debate about that in the subreddits...some say they're a body-dysmorphic Muppet, others aver H.R. to be a portly, yellow, upright frog with frightful red hair. The "H.R." stands for Highness Royal, and this comes from the creator's lips. I've never watched an episode or seen H.R. in action, but images of the creature fill me with a bittersweet sadness, H.R.'s overgrown freakish weirdness and crazy look, and a certain desperate loneliness and shocked realization of their own otherness. I feel for you, H.R. Pufnstuf!

By the way, this puzzle's great, crunchy, started off on the too easy side but kept growing more and more interesting and time consuming. A definite HR!

May I address the question Sam brought up in wordplay?

"As one who seems always to bungle the distinctions between first, second and third cousins, and who has no idea when to use the phrase “once removed,...”"

I actually learned some of this, mostly by accident.  Cousins are two people who share a set of grandparents.  Second cousins share a set of great-grandparents.  (My cousin's cousin is my second cousin, if not a first cousin.)

Third cousins share a set of great-great-grandparents, or cousins of my second cousins.

The removed part is interesting.  My first cousins children are my first cousins, once removed.  The "removed" part indicates the number of generations separating the generations.  So my first cousins grandchildren are my first cousins, twice removed.

At least I think I know this.

This is right in Nate Cardin’s bailiwick, as eight of his nine Times puzzles are Mondays or Tuesdays, and five of those eight employ English-language-quirk themes.  Nate’s got good EYES for these.

It’s a tight theme – no alternative answers yet in the comments – and props to Nate for finding six answers with the right letter counts to fit grid symmetry.  

It’s also a clean grid, and we get an extra row for no extra cost.  In addition, the theme answers are colorful, and there are lovely non-theme answers as well – OK THEN, JOTTED, TOP OFF, TRIPS UP – to brighten the grid.

Clever and fun. A sprightly way to kick off the day.  Thank you for making this, Nate!

@Andrzej

We here gathered often have robust conversations on the meaning of a common word.  Usually we can't quite reach agreement between any two of us.  (See "base hit")

I think about how language may be a dangerously inadequate way to communicate.  A killer of species who've reached "intelligence", but can't seem to get to the stage of "wise".  It's like there's a giant impedance mismatch at every stage of a talk/listen cycle when we try to communicate.

You reminded me of this because I'm aghast at how we can have laws in our society, when we can't agree on every day words the law are made of.  Or the definitions of the words the definitions are made of.  

Did you ever play the game "telephone"?  I only did once, but it was an unforgettable display of how quickly a message, passed from one to another with no quality assurance, becomes utterly, disastrously, hilariously wrong.

I'm in a cheerful mood tonight!
P. S.  I say this in a way of trying to break the news to you:  humans will have to convert to conversing in mathematics rather than language, if they want to survive.
